Voluminous

vuh-LOO-muh-nuhs -- from Latin volumen, 'a roll or scroll,' from volvere, 'to roll.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Voluminous is large in volume or space.

The professor's voluminous lecture notes filled three overflowing binders by the end of the semester.

Worked Example

A wedding gown designer adds layer after layer of tulle until the skirt is wide enough to fill an entire doorway.

That sheer bulk and size -- whether of fabric, hair, writing, or anything else -- is exactly what voluminous describes.

How Voluminous Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

capacious

capacious: able to hold a great deal

bulky

bulky: large and taking up a lot of space

Antonyms

compact

compact: small and neatly arranged

skimpy

skimpy: scant or barely enough

How Strong Is It? — capacious → voluminous → bulky

capacious vs. voluminous

capacious vs. voluminous: Capacious focuses on how much something can hold or contain, like a capacious suitcase, while voluminous more often describes the sheer visible size or fullness of something itself, like a voluminous skirt.

bulky vs. voluminous

bulky vs. voluminous: Bulky is stronger and clumsier than voluminous -- bulky suggests something large enough to be awkward or hard to carry, while voluminous simply means large in volume, which can still look graceful, like flowing robes.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — volumin-

Root — volumin-: a roll, scroll (from Latin volumen, voluminis, 'a roll' -- itself from volvere, 'to roll')

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of, characterized by (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Voluminous comes from Latin volumen, voluminis, 'a roll or scroll' -- itself from volvere, 'to roll': volumin- + -ous ('full of'). A large amount of writing had to be rolled into a bulky scroll, so voluminous came to describe anything large in volume or space.

Use the root in a new word: revolve

Root Check

Word Choice

Voluminous most often describes physical size -- clothing, hair, or containers -- but it's also commonly used for writing or paperwork that has grown unusually large, as in 'voluminous notes' or 'a voluminous report.'
